newsitem.title: TURKEY: Germany's Kinkel in EU dispute with Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Kinkel in EU dispute with Turkey.

text.p: A diplomatic rift opened between NATO allies Germany and Turkey on Wednesday as leaders traded harsh words in a row over Ankara's trade ties with the European Union.
"No European will have to bow their head to Turkey in shame," German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told German reporters on the first day of an official visit to Turkey.
Kinkel was close to calling off his visit at the last minute because of media reports quoting Erbakan as saying he should come to Turkey with his head bowed.

Erbakan told MPs of his Welfare Party on Tuesday that Turkey should be treated with more respect internationally. He blamed Europe for what he said were losses because of a customs accord with the EU that went into effect at the start of 1996.
"There will be a $5 billion loss for Turkey because it has entered the customs union ... After they have done this they will bow their heads when they talk with Turkey," Erbakan said.
EU exports to Turkey have surged under the accord, while Turkish exports to the bloc have changed little.
Erbakan, Moslem but secular Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, has promised a more independent foreign policy since he came to power last June.

"It will be very interesting to meet with him (Kinkel). Now nobody can give Turkey the 'do this, do that' treatment... The respect and treatment which the new world leader Turkey deserves will be realised," he said.

Kinkel said he would discuss what he called Turkey's "megaphone diplomacy" with Erbakan at talks later on Wednesday. "I don't feel that to be a friendly welcome. I will say that calmy and clearly," he said.
Kinkel had intended to appease Turkey over the continued EU rejection of Ankara's long-standing bid to join the bloc during his visit.
Turkey and some leading EU countries have been on a collision course since Ankara threatened in January to veto NATO's planned expansion if it were not given guarantees of EU membership.
Europe's Christian Democrat leaders, angered by the Turkish threat, said at a meeting earlier this month that Turkey's Moslem culture made it unfit to join the EU.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, who attended the meeting, took the brunt of Turkish criticism of the comments. Kinkel and other EU foreign ministers have since distanced themselves from the Christian Democrat statements.
Turkey has been an associate member of the EU since 1963 and regards it as unjust that other states, including former east European adversaries, are likely to get into the EU before it.

Millions of dollars in EU aid to Ankara under the customs union have been blocked by Turkey's traditional foe Greece over disputes in Cyprus and the Aegean and by EU states concerned about Turkey's human rights record.
Foreign ministry spokesman Sermet Atacanli said Turkey was frsutrated at the EU.
"We're not saying that relations with the EU are perfect anyway. We are saying there are problems, that the European Union has legal obligations that it has not carried out," Atacanli said.
